items.followUp: Describe the main observations and conclusion of the alpha-particle scattering experiment.

rubric.why: The setup and labeled diagram are essential parts of the experiment.
rubric.description: Names and shows the alpha-particle source, thin gold foil and fluorescent screen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct arrangement and 1 mark for a labeled diagram showing the three main components and the foil inside or in front of the screen.

rubric.why: Most alpha particles passed through the foil without deflection.
rubric.description: States that most alpha particles passed straight through.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the observation that most particles passed through undeflected.

rubric.why: The scattering observations led to the nuclear model of the atom.
rubric.description: States that some particles were deflected and a very small number bounced back, showing that the atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the deflection and rebound observations with the conclusion about the nucleus.

modelAnswer: An alpha-particle source was placed in a lead block with a narrow slit so that a thin beam of alpha particles was directed at a very thin gold foil.
A circular fluorescent screen coated with zinc sulphide (ZnS) surrounded the foil and produced flashes where alpha particles struck it.
Diagram: α-source in lead block → narrow beam → thin gold foil; circular ZnS screen around the foil. Most α-particles pass straight through; a few are deflected; very few return backwards.
Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil; a few were deflected, and a very small number bounced back.
Rutherford concluded that atoms are mostly empty space and have a very small, dense, positively charged nucleus.

items.followUp: How many moles are present in 24 g of carbon?

rubric.why: The mole calculation uses the mass divided by the molar mass.
rubric.description: States the relation between moles, mass and molar mass.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula.

rubric.why: Carbon has a molar mass of 12 g mol⁻¹, giving 0.75 mol for 9 g.
rubric.description: Substitutes the carbon mass and gives the answer with its unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct numerical result with mol as the unit.

modelAnswer: Given: mass of carbon, m = 9 g; molar mass of carbon, M = 12 g mol⁻¹.
Formula: n = m/M.
Substitution: n = 9 g ÷ 12 g mol⁻¹ = 0.75 mol.
Answer: 0.75 mol of carbon.

items.followUp: How many atoms are present in a diatomic molecule? Give one example.

rubric.why: A diatomic molecule contains two atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is a molecule made of two atoms.

rubric.why: A triatomic molecule contains three atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is a molecule made of three atoms.

modelAnswer: A diatomic molecule is a molecule made up of two atoms, for example, H₂.
A triatomic molecule is a molecule made up of three atoms, for example, H₂O.

items.followUp: How many electrons can the M shell accommodate? Give an example of an element with electrons in that shell.

rubric.why: The K shell accommodates 2 electrons and the L shell accommodates 8 electrons.
rubric.description: Gives the capacities of both shells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for K = 2 and L = 8 electrons.

rubric.why: Neon has the shell arrangement 2,8, illustrating the K and L shell capacities.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example with its electron arrangement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example such as neon (2,8).

modelAnswer: The K shell can accommodate 2 electrons and the L shell can accommodate 8 electrons.
Example: Neon has the electron arrangement 2,8; its K shell contains 2 electrons and its L shell contains 8 electrons.

items.followUp: State one difference between Thomson’s model of the atom and Rutherford’s nuclear model.

rubric.why: In the plum pudding model, positive charge is spread throughout the atom.
rubric.description: Identifies the atom as a positively charged sphere.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that positive charge forms a sphere or is spread throughout the atom.

rubric.why: The model pictures electrons embedded in the positive sphere, like plums in pudding.
rubric.description: Describes the embedded electrons or the plum-pudding analogy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons are embedded in the positive sphere.

modelAnswer: Thomson’s “Plum Pudding” theory described the atom as a positively charged sphere.
Electrons were embedded in this sphere, like plums in a pudding, so the positive and negative charges balanced.

items.followUp: What are the periods in the periodic table, and how many periods are there?

rubric.why: Periods are the horizontal rows of the periodic table.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying periods as horizontal rows.

rubric.why: Groups are the vertical columns of the periodic table.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying groups as vertical columns.

modelAnswer: Groups are the vertical columns in the periodic table.
Periods are the horizontal rows in the periodic table.

items.followUp: Describe how atomic size changes across a period and down a group.

rubric.why: Electronegativity generally increases from left to right across a period.
rubric.description: Gives the trend across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electronegativity increases across a period.

rubric.why: Electronegativity generally decreases down a group.
rubric.description: Gives the trend down a group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electronegativity decreases down a group.

modelAnswer: Across a period, electronegativity generally increases from left to right.
Down a group, electronegativity generally decreases from top to bottom.

items.followUp: Define atomic number and state its usual symbol.

rubric.why: Atomic radius describes the size of an atom; it may be expressed as the distance from the nucleus to the outermost shell or, for bonded identical atoms, half the distance between their nuclei.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an accepted definition of atomic radius.

rubric.why: Atomic radius is commonly expressed in nanometres or picometres.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct unit such as nm or pm.

modelAnswer: Atomic radius is the distance from the nucleus to the outermost electron shell of an atom; for two bonded identical atoms, it is half the distance between their nuclei.
Its unit is the nanometre (nm); it is also commonly expressed in picometres (pm).
